utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We did indicate that we would make a determination in relation to the admission of P407. Before making a final decision on that, I would ask Mr. Marcussen if he would explain to us again the use he considers that we might make of this as a freestanding document, and secondly, to make any further submissions he wants to make about its general reliability. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Now, as for the use of the document, as I indicated yesterday, it's the Prosecution's submission that this particular document is -- is a good reference document, a sort of one-stop shop which gives an overview of incidents occurring in Kosovo both in terms of crimes committed by the KLA and acts considered -- or concern -- committed by the Serb side. During the case there has already been a number of references to events and acts carried out by both sides in this conflict. There have been, yesterday, for example, an issue of whether or not there was a rise or fall in the conflicts, and this particular document gives an overview on a day-by-day basis of what was going on in Kosovo. So we would submit, as I said, this is a one-stop shop. Although it is a long document, it gives, in a relatively brief form, an overview of the events in Kosovo for the period of time that the KVM was in Kosovo, plus some time after Kosovo -- sorry, after the KVM had left Kosovo. As to the reliability of the information, we got a fairly extensive explanation by General Drewienkiewicz yesterday as to how this -- this document was created, how there were written reports being sent up from field offices of the KVM to the Fusion Cell which was responsible for compiling all this information, assessing the reliability of the information. This assessment was made by trained analysts, principally, former intelligence officers who have experience in assessing this kind of information, and when deemed credible, the information was included in the various reports that the KVM did, including the blue book. There has been a number of -- there have been a number of documents that have been referred to both by the Prosecution and the Defence during this case where some of the underlying documents and also excerpts of the blue book have been presented as being a true reflection of events on certain days in Kosovo. To a large extent, it seems that the contents of this book is actually already accepted by both parties. I would submit that there's a difference between the concern that has been raised in the context of "As Seen, As Told" and then the blue book, in that one of the concerns in "As Seen, As Told" has been whether or not the underlying -- witness evidence that has been summarised in "As Seen, As Told" is real liable. I think this is a very different kind of document in that we have direct recordings coming from KVM monitors on the ground in Kosovo reporting to the Fusion Cell, who then compiled the information and disseminated in the blue book. And the entries in the blue book are such that when hearsay information is passed on, that's normally reflected in the entries. So on this basis, we submit that the evidence is reliability and it's the way it can be assessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is all the underlying material disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There is a vast of -- a vast amount of KVM and OSCE material that has been disclosed. I would be reluctant to state that all the underlying material has been disclosed. I'm simply not certain of that. But there have has been a lot disclosed and certainly, I think, about the key events that have been discussed Vukovar, Racak. Also evidence about some of the group heard of individual killings and, I think, at one point, we heard about the killing of an individual policeman and attempts by his family to rescue this -- sorry, a soldier who got caught by the KLA and attempts to rescue him. That was brought up in cross-examination and some of these documents relied on it. A lot of that material has been disclosed at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But where there's a report in a paragraph that says KVM patrol came across something and reported what they saw, perhaps people shot, an investigation going on, is there an underlying report that will be available on that, or does that vary from example to example?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: As I said, I have -- I'm not in a position to say that for every single incident there is an underlying report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it then that when it comes to the submissions in due course where a report in the blue book has never been referred to and explored, there's no question of you inviting us to give it weight as helping to establish a fact or as the basis for drawing a conclusion? You simply view it as background material that gives a general picture of events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think one -- one of the issues in this case, and I think we see it in one way developing more and more on the evidence, some of the trends and developments in -- in the -- how things unfolded in Kosovo, and we would be happy if the document is admitted as a background document. I suspect it might be a useful document, actually, later on to get a picture of development in activity in Kosovo and, therefore, to be used as part of the evidence to be considered when some of the sort of broader inferences are to be made in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. You may come across a passage that said yesterday there were 50.000 people amassed on the border of Macedonia and now they've disappeared, and it looks as though they've maybe gone home. Would you invite us, without that having been explored at all, to use it as a piece of material that would support the idea that there were 50.000 people amassing on the border on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In principle, I would say yes, but I would do it with this modification, though: I think at the end of the day when the Chamber is to assess the evidence in this case and look at the different facts of the case, you would be looking at the totality of the evidence on record, and there are some issues that are more significant than others. And I think for sort of the bigger issues there will be more evidence available than the blue book and, therefore, it would just be one piece of a puzzle on some of these things. But there are smaller incidents reported in the book where I think it might be appropriate simply to accept the entry in the blue book as being a correct reflection of the events. I mentioned this example that had been brought up on cross-examination, I think, a number of times, where, as I understand, we all agree a soldier straight off leaving his post, going home, he went home in his uniform, not with his weapon, but he went home in his uniform, he was intercepted by the KLA. Two family members went out to try to recover their son. They got shot. Incident reported. Now, that's a small piece in the puzzle, and on something like that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, my recollection is that the only witness whose spoken to that denied that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Or denied knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And -- no, not denied knowledge of it. He was prepared to give you an assertion that the events were different from those being portrayed and perhaps generally agreed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But -- yeah. I mean, as I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A better example might be the shooting of the last Serb in the village near Podujevo where you may -- there may be some agreement, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We would -- as a general matter, we would submit that the contents of the report is sufficiently reliable to be used as evidence of the facts on the ground in Kosovo. There might be instances where things have not been correctly reported, and that is coming out in the evidence, but in general, we would submit that the report can be accepted as reflection of what was going on in Kosovo. But as I said, if the Chamber thinks that is not an appropriate way to use the document, we would nonetheless submit that, at least for reference purposes, this can be used and would be used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan, do you want to add anything to what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd just like to briefly respond to what my learned friend just said. First off, this document is not accepted by the parties. We contest this document. Specific portions of it have been used during the examination and cross-examination, and when these specific portions are used and put specifically to witnesses at different times, we say that's completely in compliance with this letter and the spirit of your order of July on the use of these voluminous documents. We contest the underlying evidence that supports this. We contest both the objectivity of the KVM. We object as well, to give one example, the ability of the KVM to observe the situation accurately. General DZ said that there were several hundred KLA. We heard that the Chief of Staff said there were 18.000 KLA. I won't comment any further on that. I illustrate that to say that we don't rely on -- the underlying reports furnished by KVM are both biased and unreliable. There's portions of this report dealing with Racak. Racak is not in the indictment. It's struck from General DZ's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me just make one thing clear about cross-examination. Even where it is used in cross-examination, if -- if the witness doesn't accept the propositions being put to him, then the matter hasn't been advanced any and the document's as worthless in that situation as it was before it started. Obviously, the opportunity remains for you to rectify that by establishing the events in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your point's well taken, Your Honour. In addition, I would say that the Prosecution cannot demonstrate that the underlying material has been disclosed or is complete and has no ability to verify that underlying material. We say, as we said yesterday, picking up on what my learned friends have said, that your order of the -- of July was -- was designed to avoid having irrelevant material with no probative value in the record, which would only lead to confusion at the end of the case to say whether or not and disputes over whether or not a certain portion or section of a document should come in. When it's dealt the other way, as you say, where it's either adopted by a witness as being accurate and truthful or through stipulation, then there will be a neater record and a tidier arguments at the end of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Our general impression is that this material, and I use this relatively, that this material bears the impression of being more reliable than the Human Rights' material. That's a matter of impression and relativity. I'm not suggesting that it makes it reliable in the sense of justifying admitting it, but it makes it look more generally reliable as we see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I've already stated our position about how we feel about the KVM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, is there anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to touch on the last point Your Honour made. I tend to view this report in two phases. There was the phase when the KVM was on the ground and when the observations were based upon what they saw and there is the phase after they withdrew that's based upon secondhand information. So I stress that's something that needs to be taken into account, particularly when we see from the general's testimony yesterday, that they look at the reliability in terms of whether something is confirmed by other sources and without knowing what those sources are and in fact having some indications that some of the sources they used are indeed the Human Rights Watch -- the human rights groups analyses that has been found to be questionable, then we really can't -- we can't really appraise the reliability of those aspects of the report that come after the withdrawal of the -- of the KVM mission. And as for the parts prior, that's -- that's the provenance of cross-examination to examine certain of those -- those incidents to see -- to test the knowledge of various witnesses we have had coming here from the KVM. But I think with respect to the events that are reported as happening after the withdrawal is virtually impossible to test that material with any of the witnesses since it is secondhand and we really don't know what all the sources are so as to be able to challenge it. So that's one of the -- one of the problems. And I just stress that we have to kind of look at the report in those two veins, the vein of part of the report that was undertaken while they were on the ground and the part that was undertaken while they were outside of the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let me give a very limited reply, and I think I'll limit it to two things. I do think that in some of the ways the cross-examination on both the blue book and the underlying documents has been carried out. The -- these documents are being presented as a correct reflection of what took place on the ground and certain facts about an event has been put to a witness and the witness has basically being said well, this is what happened, isn't it? An example is the use of Exhibit 3D363 on the 7th of November at page 6033, where Zyrapi is being asked, Witness Bislim Zyrapi is being asked about a report. And he's being, basically, so this is the facts. So that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But does he accept it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: On this occasion he says no, I don't know about the incident. But it's being used as a presentation of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't take the matter anywhere. Maybe it was used in cross-examination, I don't doubt that, and that would apply when you come to cross-examine, too, but what it amounts to depends in that sort of situation on what the witness is prepared to accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the second -- the second point is with respect to what the witness said yesterday about consultation of human rights people. It's my understanding at page 7762 he says, "Well, we drew on the experience of human rights people as well because we were entering areas that we frankly hadn't got a lot of experience of." Now, the way I understood that at least was that these were on legal issues -- what amounts of human rights violations in what kind of situation. I mean these were military people. That was their primary [indiscernible]. Maybe, otherwise, that's something that should be clarified with the witness but it's not my understanding of the evidence that the general indicated that they were reporting what the human rights people told them they had been told by refugees. So that would be my -- my -- my second point. Maybe if I may add a third point which is more of a technical thing about how our record looks. A lot of -- well, some excerpts of the blue book, a lot of OSCE and other documents that have been used in cross-examination, I understand the point that has been made about the limited nature of the admission of the documents, but when you look in e-court, all the documents are simply marked as admitted on a certain date and as an exhibit. So depending on how you -- you rule on this issue, it might be something we need to look into just in terms of an illustrative issue and also these kind of documents can also be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, that's not the case. The exhibit has to be there for the purpose for which it was used and the Trial Chamber will be able to identify that clearly from the whole context of the transcript when it comes to deliberate. It doesn't follow that simply because it got in in a cross-examination of a witness who denied that it was accurate that the Trial Chamber will then look at it as a matter of accuracy. We would have to accept there's no evidence there in relation to it. But to understand the point, we need the exhibit. If later, evidence comes along from another source to confirm the accuracy of the report, it's still not the report we will be relying upon, unless, in some way, the witness is invited to confirm the report, then, of course, it will be become part of the positive evidence that the Defence could rely on on that point. But we're not getting into an area where we're going to review every exhibit and make it clear when it should already be abundantly clear the purpose for which that exhibit has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Since it was a Defence objection, the last word should be with the Defence. Is there anything else that's to be said on this? No. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber considers this material to be different from the human rights material. This is a record compiled by a body on the ground in Kosovo of the evidence -- the material, rather, that they could accumulate on events as they were occurring and being reported to them. It was a duty to do it. So they were presenting a compilation of their findings throughout that period. So it has a value. There is no doubt this material has some stand-alone merit. However, the Trial Chamber do not consider this material to be an appropriate basis for a finding in fact to be made or for a conclusion on fact to be drawn without the matter having been explored in evidence, so that we can have a proper view of the reliability of that individual piece of material in its context. On the other hand, we do think that it's legitimate to look at the way in which the material was compiled and in the context of the matters which Mr. Marcussen identified yesterday and repeated today, namely, an overview, for an overview of the developing situation on the ground in Kosovo. Now, that is the limit of the use that the Trial Chamber will make of the material insofar as it is not explored in evidence, and you can rely on us not saying that because there's been a witness spoke to an event and it's also recorded in the book, you can rely on us not saying, well, the record and the book corroborates the event unless the matter has been explored in oral evidence in some way. Now, I hope that gives suitable guidance. We think it would be irresponsible of us to reject this document out of hand as inadmissible in view of the way in which it was being compiled, the purpose for which it was being compiled, and the circumstances in which it was compiled. Now, there are other items which there maybe some doubt about from yesterday. For the avoidance of doubt, the various exhibits which were explored to some extent with the witness were plainly admitted as we went along, and they were admitted to the extent that the evidence dealt with them. They may have been almost exclusively in the first instance to demonstrate the system and for no other purpose, but to the extent that the facts were also explored, then they fall within the category I've just been outlining. Mr. Marcussen then listed a number that he would wish to have admitted but said he would make submissions in writing in relation to these as I understand it, so some of them have not been dealt with and there will be an opportunity for the Defence to deal with these particular ones which were from P659, a series of numbers. One of the exhibits attached to the statement of the witness is a plan of Racak, which I think is P73 and is known as DZB in the exhibits. There is no basis for exhibiting that, I don't think, and therefore, that will not be part of the admitted documents. And you can rely on us excluding from consideration any of the documents in P407 that relate to the particular events in the village of Racak. Now, does that deal -- I think that deals with all outstanding matters in relation to the exhibits with the witness, and we can now return to the evidence. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the delay, but as I explained to you as I came into the courtroom earlier, there would be this delay while we dealt with the matter that was outstanding from yesterday. Your cross-examination will now resume. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. How are you today?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Looking forward to some more insights on counter-revolutionary war from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're finished with that, General. We'll have some insights on some other things today, I hope. I want to talk to you, first, about NATO and ACTORD which you mentioned briefly in your direct testimony yesterday. An ACTORD is an order basically to NATO forces to raise the level of their readiness from a former level, I think, that was called act-warn to a level where attack can be carried out within a period of 96 hours. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that's approximately right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Some of my information comes from Wesley Clark's book "Waging Modern War" where he talks about that and mentioned that when NATO issued their ACTORD that the strike aircraft were already assembled in Italy to carry out that ACTORD if necessary. And says about that the ACTORD directed airstrikes after 96 hours with the understanding that any further suspension would have to be voted by the council. I don't know whether you know about that or not.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I haven't served in -- in shape in that part of NATO, so I think -- I think I would defer to the Supreme Commander on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I don't know if you know the dates, but the information I have indicates that the Holbrooke-Milosevic meeting that resulted in the agreement that eventually became the OSCE-FRY agreement for your mission was held -- concluded, the agreement concluded on the 12th of October, and that Mr. Holbrooke then went to Brussels and met with the NATO council and explained to them that he'd arrived at this agreement with Milosevic, and at the conclusion of that meeting on the evening of October 13th, the ACTORD was issued. Do you know about that? Do you remember those dates? Can you confirm that information?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, because -- I mean, my source of information at that stage in October was -- was the open press. I was at home in England on leave having been in Bosnia until the middle of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: So I -- I wasn't getting daily updates from SACEUR.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you remember, you could have -- or if you looked, you could have, I think, learned from the public press about the meeting on the 12th and about the ACTORD issuance on the 13th, but I can understand when you don't remember those dates. I wouldn't be able to. I'd be surprised if you could.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I'm certainly aware that the act warn had been issued and then an ACTORD was issued because it was very significant. It was the first time it had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The point I am trying to make and if you can't help me with it, just tell me, is that first came the agreement with Milosevic for a cease-fire and the other matters that were discussed, and then after that came the ACTORD.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I just don't know what that sequencing is, and I -- if I was looking for dates, I wouldn't go to "Waging Modern War" because it doesn't have dates in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It has a few but not very many, you're right. I'd like you to take a look at an exhibit that you were shown yesterday, P2535, and I'm interested in page 2 of that exhibit. And we'll have to blow it up a little bit. There's a bullet point that starts with "I will then conduct the inspection."

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this is a meeting that you're having with General Ojdanic on the 27th of November where you're talking about the kind of inspections that you propose to carry out, and what you apparently told him, if your bullet points are correct here, that you would be involved in checking and counting all personnel, heavy weapons and equipment, even going into barracks and work areas. You said, "I will bring various items of equipment to enable me to effectively complete the inspection. For instance, GPS, camera, tape recorder. I will take photos and record serial numbers of heavy weapons or other equipment as I deem necessary. I have no intention of interfering with routine activities at the inspected unit, but I will conduct a thorough inspection." Now, the first thing that we know was that on November 27th, the ACTORD was still in effect. It had not been withdrawn, had it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah. It was parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The second thing that we know is that if you have a GPS, especially a GPS -- I can't remember whether the military satellites had been opened to the public by then or not, but if you had a GPS with access to those military satellites, you could pinpoint things down to within a couple of metres, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so with that GPS, you could walk up to a tank and record the coordinates of that tank and someone could find it with those coordinates pretty easily couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, provided it hadn't moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And target it with a missile?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that information, had you been able to acquire it, would have been quite helpful to NATO as they initiated their bombing campaign as targeting information, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: If they had done that and if that information had been passed to them, neither of which happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think -- I suggest to you that it's really unimportant whether that happened or not. What's important is whether there was a perception among the Serb forces, General Ojdanic and the other persons in charge, that that information could be passed on to NATO. And I think anybody, don't you, would be foolish to allow in a situation where ACTORD is in effect, where an attack can occur within 96 hours, would be foolish to allow at that kind of a pinpoint accuracy inspection of their military hardware, their tanks and artillery and perhaps missile sites? I mean, that would be a huge mistake, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Not if they were already flying overhead able to do that for themselves all the time, which they were, because that was the NATO version of the air -- NATO air Verification Mission was entitled to do just that. So if they wanted to collect that information for targeting purposes, they had plenty of means to do it on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if those --

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They didn't need us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And if they could observe all these things from overflights then there would be no need for you to do the inspection, and that wouldn't make sense, because the overflights were part of the agreement, just an complementation of part of the agreement, the air force part of that agreement. So it would make no sense for you to go look at the tanks if they were looking at them from the air. It's the ones that they couldn't see from the air that you wanted to go look at wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That wasn't at all in our minds, no. NATO wasn't sending us all the results of all their photos, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But their purpose, there was an agreement signed by General Clark, and I'm sure you're familiar with that agreement, that was part of the agreement with Milosevic to involve flights over Kosovo, reconnaissance flights, surveillance flights, was part of the same agreement. So they are simply implementing that part by flying over and you're implementing the part on the ground, except the part on the ground didn't permit you to go look at their tanks did it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Show me.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: We were there to ensure that the people, the troops on the ground, the troop levels on the ground had returned to their -- their earlier state and one of our great problems was that at no stage did we get a proper formal baseline given to us. Absent that, we had to count what we saw where we saw it. That wasn't a cooperative approach by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me -- I'm not sure I want to go through this, again, but I would like you to look at P432. Okay. We'll stay there on the first page. First thing I want you to notice is that this is the agreement, the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission agreement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yep, got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On the first page it says that one of the chapeau preamble parts of this is it's devoted to the respect of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states in the region; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go look further into the document, I think it's on page 3 that we want to be now, so it's like two pages past where we are. Yeah, to verify compliance by all parties in Kosovo with UN Security Council Resolution 1199. So that was part of your task to verify compliance with that Resolution; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you go down under "specific terms of reference," the Verification Mission will travel throughout Kosovo to verify the maintenance of the cease-fire by all elements; right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were given in the agreement an assurance that you'd be able to travel throughout Kosovo unimpeded for the purpose -- for the purpose of verifying the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: You'll note that we had free -- we were given full freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo at all times, which we certainly didn't get.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But the purpose was to verify the cease-fire, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. But it -- but it was to -- it's a separate sentence. "Mission personnel will have full freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo at all times and it's not restricted."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, but it doesn't say that you can go into barracks and look at tanks and take a GPS and put in their coordinates and do all of that. That's not in there anywhere that gives you that detailed a right of inspection, is it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It doesn't say we can't. It says full freedom of movement and full freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo at all times in English means we can go where we want, when we want, and that was how we understood it, and that was how we described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if the agreement had had one paragraph that said this agreement is to provide for verification of a cease-fire, it -- your view is that you could then do anything because it didn't say you couldn't?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. We would have discussed it and we'd have agreed what we were going to do, and the head of mission would have said, yes, that's okay. I agree with that concept. This concept of how we were going to do inspections was discussed with the head of mission, and he agreed it. He also wrote a letter, you'll recall, which detailed that in great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I understand that you're position now is if it doesn't prohibit your doing something you're just free to go ahead and do it. And I'm satisfied with that position because my understanding has always been that agreements give you permission to do things especially in a sovereign country, and if you don't have those permissions you're not permitted to do them. But I understand it's your position and I will accept it from you, although I don't agree with it.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, may I remind you that inspections of weapon sites happened throughout this region all the time, and this is something which is commonplace. So it wasn't as though there were no inspections of this sovereign state ever. There were arms control inspections in various forms throughout -- throughout the time and throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, yes, but there were agreements for doing that, specific agreements permitting that. This agreement was a different agreement. It was to verify a cease-fire and you don't have to go look at their weapons to verify whether they're shooting each other or not. And that was the disagreement that was going on between you and the Serb authorities. What --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are kindly asking you to slow down. We're having enormous difficulties trying to interpret what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Which of you was right about that is not very important, I don't think, as long as you understand that there was a dispute because the agreement was not clear.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I do understand that, and I can help you, I think, by saying that when we first looked at one of the VJ company positions, we did GPS everything, and this then came up in discussion with the authorities, and as a result of that, I gave instructions that we should not do that any more in order not to -- to have one less thing that we were arguing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was after the 27th of November?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Indeed. That was in the first week of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I don't regard the witness as having said simply that it was permissible because it was not prohibited. He's plainly relied on the positive part that gives him full freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in the question I asked was it didn't give you permission to go into barracks and do the kind of inspection you were talking about, and he said it didn't prohibit us from doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but I mean, the plain English is not something that has any restriction on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's his position, that if it's not restricted, then he can do it and that's what I'm quarreling with, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What then is -- are you suggesting that access throughout Kosovo means?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The 1199 says that there should be access throughout Kosovo. This agreement says there should be access throughout Kosovo to verify a cease-fire. That's what it's about. And to see whether people are shooting each other or not -- at each other or not, it's important that you have access throughout Kosovo, but you don't have to go into barracks to see if people are shooting each other. That's -- that's my position. So that access is important. That means access to the roads, to be able to go down the roads, to go to the villages, to go to the places, to see if there are violations of the cease-fire, and I think that's what this agreement is talking about. I think it's clear on its face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And whether we're having a lawsuit about it, I think that would have to be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll hear the submissions later. Mr. Drewienkiewicz, where does the idea come from that there had to be a baseline established and that one of the real issues here was maintaining levels no higher than they were than when the mission arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was as you say, that all of the different discussions that led to essentially the three documents, the -- the OSCE-FRY agreement, the agreement with General Wesley Clark, and the agreement on MUP check-points that was, I think, the Djordjevic-Burns agreement, those three all contained references to the situation before essentially reinforcements were brought in from outside to Kosovo over the course of the summer, that the troop and police levels should be back to their original levels. Now, if we weren't able to know what the original level was, then how were we to verify whether or not compliance was in place or not? That was the point. In arms control, you always need a baseline. If you're going to check anything, you need a baseline. You need to know what's normal, and that's what we were asking for constantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to a different subject now. I want to talk about General Loncar. In your statement, at paragraph 171, you indicated you had a good working relationship with General Loncar; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the -- in fact, in the Milosevic case, at page 2841, you said this: "Loncar was very well-informed. He certainly appeared to have good communications with people in the field and was generally one of the first to know when something happened. He also seemed better able to get decisions from Belgrade, and either as a result of a telephone call or he sometimes said something to me that he had spent the night driving to Belgrade and back." True?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So from that it appears you had a great deal of respect for General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At paragraph 69 of your statement, and you talked about this a little bit in your evidence yesterday, you spoke to Loncar about meeting General Pavkovic, and you were told that it was not possible, that you needed to deal with Loncar directly. Now, you don't know who actually made this decision that you were not going to be meeting with General Pavkovic, do you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I was told by Loncar, to the best of my recollection, that it was a decision from -- from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it you have no knowledge at all whether General Pavkovic was ever aware of this situation at all?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I did not discuss it with General Pavkovic, I agree. It would have been quite difficult for me to take the corps headquarters by storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But, I mean, you don't know if he knew where this situation where you requested to meet with him had been denied. You don't know that he was ever informed of that, do you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk to you now for a bit about the -- I guess I'll call it the -- the attitude that you approached this mission in Kosovo with, and I'm going to suggest to you, just to be fair, that you went there with a -- with a bias that affected your work, which continues today, I believe. Yesterday, we talked about your estimate of the number of KLA fighters in March of 1999, and you told us that it was in the hundreds, less than a thousand, and I suggest to you that you're giving us this relatively small estimate of the KLA force to try to show to this Trial Chamber that the VJ was overwhelming the KLA. The KLA was not a threat of any kind, and that any reaction by the JNA -- by the VJ or the police were just overreactions.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Those aren't my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you did arrive there with a bias, didn't you, against Serbs, pro-KLA?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I did not. I promise you I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, with regard to this issue, it's difficult to understand why you insist on such a small number of KLA. You told us yesterday that the KLA commander's testimony of 17 to 18.000 KLA soldiers in March was not true?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I said I didn't believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. You said that between December and March the numbers of KLA fighters was increasing.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So now I think you're probably going to tell this Chamber that Colonel Ciaglinski is also not believable, because when he was here, at page 6911, asked about the Podujevo area at the end of December, how many KLA were in that area, he said there were 1 to 2.000 fighters, well-armed, just in that area, Podujevo. So you don't believe that either, do you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't ever go into any KLA areas. I did. The most I ever saw there was about 20, and the first time I went into a KLA area, which was on Christmas Day, the 25th of December, 1998, I remember that they had assembled to impress us, the armoured might of the KLA, and there were 10 guys and they weren't all with the same weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, didn't he go into Podujevo to try to defuse a situation, defuse a situation at some risk to his own life, and wouldn't that have given him some sense that there were 1.000 to 2.000 fighters there? What do you mean he never went where there were KLA?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: He tended to stay on the Serb side because he was my liaison to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But he did go into Podujevo, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: He went up onto the hill above Podujevo and he may have seen some of the KLA fighters. There certainly weren't 1 to 2.000 there, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Wasn't that where he was decorated for going in and taking someone out?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I personally wrote it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So we shouldn't believe him either?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, let -- I think I need to be quite -- quite specific here. What I'm talking about is what I would call the hardcore fighters, which I would describe as the football team that's on the field. I'm not talking about the supporters that turn up to the terraces. And as I said yesterday, if a specific area was attacked, then it was quite possible that the people that lived there would defend that village, but they didn't see themselves as available to the KLA as part of the core forces, the core forces of the KLA. Those people that sat on the top of the hills were several hundred, to the best of my knowledge, and that would be supported by my conversations with the various people that went in and out of those locations on a regular basis. Around those, if you went to a village, you could get locals to turn out to defend their village because they were being attacked by forces that they felt were not on their side. So you could get people to defend their village who I don't describe as being in the KLA. They were supporting the KLA, but they were not the core KLA. If you had gone up the hills and taken up the few hundred that were on the top of the hills, then the KLA would have gone away. When the border ambush happened in December, we have it on fairly good authority that there were 140 people in that convoy, and of those 140, my reports tell me that less than 10 were proper fighters. The others were impressed people. So what I'm talking about is the people that were the real danger, and that, I would still say, was less than a thousand. Now, once you get to the end of the game, all the supporters run onto the football field, and so do they at the end of a campaign. And so once you get to June, of course there are thousands of KLA. Everybody's in the KLA, because the perception is that the KLA is now a going concern. But in the time that they were fighting on the tops of the hills -- when I went up to the top of Stari Trg, I never saw more than 20 people, and I stick to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked about that convoy of 140 people, and you said, "The others were impressed people." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They were people who had been contacted in their villages. They had been threatened that they would be killed if they did not go to Albania to join the KLA. They were -- so they went to Albania because they were fearful that they would be killed. There they received about a day and a half or two day's worth of training, were given a rucksack and told to haul their rucksack into Kosovo, which they did. And when they were ambushed, they didn't know how to use their weapons and they ran away, and many of them were killed. And the nine that were taken prisoner and were held in the gaol in Nis that Richard Ciaglinski went and talked to told him that, and I never heard any denial of it from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, to be fair with you because of the answer you've given, I want to share with you the exact testimony given by Ciaglinski. A question was asked of him: "With regard to the incident dated 27th of December, when thanks to your invention a Serb civilian was released, you stated also that in that region," that would be Podujevo, "there was a high concentration of the members of the so-called KLA ranging from 1.000 to 2.000 fighters, that they were well-armed; is that correct?" His answer is, "It is correct." Now, he didn't talk about those being village people who were just defending themselves or coming out of the village or something. He talked about these as being well-armed KLA fighters. You don't agree with that, do you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: If they had been well-armed, then the first time that Walker went into a KLA location, which was when I was with him, and they wanted to impress him, they wouldn't have put the 10 people that I saw out on parade and they would have made jolly sure that they all had matching weapons and they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: 25th of December, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Things were ranging rapidly, though, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They were getting better armed and they were getting better equipment?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they wound up with these 50-calibre sniper rifles, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: So you tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know. You were there to verify things and look at things and you don't know that they had 50-calibre sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They weren't making arms declarations onto a baseline either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You weren't inspecting them either, were you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: We weren't able to inspect them formally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to go on to something else. On the 15th of January, 1999, there was an agreement that the KVM would escort MUP into the Decani area for the change over of their forward posts in order to ensure no reinforcement of those posts. Two orange KVM vehicles led two MUP vehicles and then someone fired on those vehicles wounding one international staff member and one local staff member. I'm sure you remember that incident. You speak about it in paragraph 140 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it vividly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you learned of this incident, your reaction was to confront General Loncar and suggest to him that MUP had set that up to make it look like KLA was responsible, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That's a shorthand. The incident happened on the Friday afternoon. I saw General Loncar the next morning, having spent a large proportion of the night trying to put together what had happened. Part of this -- my reason for thinking that we may have been set up by the Serbs was that Ciaglinski had been part of this group and had been talking to the MUP who were standing around because there was a lot of standing around while everyone was working out what was going to happen next, and there had been a lot of discussion about how well armoured the vehicles were and did they think the -- the toughened glass on the jeeps, which was all it was, really, would -- would withstand bullets. At the moment that the vehicles were fired at, it could have come from anywhere. It did come from the KLA. They admitted it, and when they did admit it, we pressed them very hard to admit it publicly, and I was quite clear that that was what had happened. That all happened over a period of several days. It was while Racak was going on, incidentally, so there were a few other diversions to -- to make sure that we didn't concentrate only on this, but at the time, 18 hours after the incident, I had concluded that the balance of probability at that stage was that it had been a set-up by the Serbs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. It took you a long time to answer yes, didn't it? But that was what you did. You went to Loncar and you accused him of that being a Serb trick to make it look like the KLA had done it. And then you maintained that position until the KLA finally publicly admitted that they'd done it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. And I was also the person who was pressuring, demanding the KLA that they did admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when did you go apologise to General Loncar for that false accusation?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I am sure that I said it to him at some stage. This was rather overtaken by the Racak event, so we weren't really -- well, that -- well, it got overtaken by Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is an Exhibit P638 that I'd like you to see. I'm sure you didn't write this press release. It talks about a serious breach of a cease-fire near Prizren on 8 January of 1999. The MUP informed KVM of an attack on MUP vehicles at 11.30, and that attack was confirmed by KVM's own patrols. And then the last paragraph is curious. Instead of going off and complaining to the KLA that they should stop attacking MUP vehicles, what KVM did was appeal to both sides not to commit provocations and to avoid further escalation. So when you suspect the Serbs are responsible, you go yell at General Loncar. And when you suspect the KLA is responsible, you appeal to both sides to cool it. Now, isn't there a bias there?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry. I was involved in the writing of that press release because it was an a group effort by all of the senior leadership of the KVM. Ambassador Walker was back in the States, and so ambassador Gabrielle Keller was in charge. And clearly this was very serious, and it was very serious not simply because of what had happened, it was serious because it was the most -- the biggest daylight event that the KLA had staged in our time there, and we were very concerned this it. We were also very concerned that the Serb reaction should be reaction and not overreaction, because up until then, we had observed that every time there was provocation by the KLA that the Serbs tended to overreact, and that is why the last paragraph is written the way it was written. And having sat around a table composing this press release, we, as the acting head of the mission, Keller, and the deputy heads of the mission that were present said, "Are we all comfortable? Are we all signed up to? Do we all agree that this is the press release that should go out?" And we all said, "Yes." And if you'd like to ask Ambassador Keller, I'm sure he would confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I knew where he was, I'd ask him. I'm trying to find him. Another incident was one that was discussed briefly yesterday, and that was the Panda Bar incident where four Serb youths were killed, seven were wounded, and your reaction to that was one of the possibilities would be that the Serbs had done that to show the Kosovar Albanians to be child killers. So you actually were -- were publicly expounding the proposition that the Serbs would kill their own children to make it look like the KLA were bad guys. That was the position you were taking, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I'd served in the Balkans for some time at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you took that with absolutely no evidence, didn't you? Zero.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: None of the propositions had any evidence. They were all speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But that was a pretty extreme speculation with no evidence for you to say in the position you had to accuse the Serbs of killing their own children, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You can sit there and say that with a straight face?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I can because I'd served in the Balkans for over 20 months by that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your supplemental information sheet you now take the position that you no longer believe the Serbs were responsible. What is it you've learned recently to cause you to change your mind about that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I think on -- on the -- thinking about it, on the balance of probability, I think it was a drive-by shooting that just happened to be at that moment, and the reaction that -- that the killing of those children caused was -- was such that I felt that that probably would not have been something that would have been done knowingly by the Serbs. So on reflection, I felt more strongly that it was a drive-by shooting by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would have been nice if you had that kind of reflection initially wouldn't it, before you made such a wild accusation?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I didn't make the accusation. I think I -- I wrote it on a note to myself, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You now think this was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I was actually trying to look in the statement for support for the proposition that the general publicly took this stance. I wanted to ask Mr. Ackerman if there was a reference for that. Otherwise, I think, it's -- the general hasn't explained that he thought there were three options.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, Your Honour, I think it was publicly taken in the Milosevic trial if nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That's giving evidence after the events about what he thought at the time. That is not that he took a stand in 1999 and publicly said there were three options.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your position now is that this was a KLA drive-by shooting probably related to crime rather than anything else. I think that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What do you mean related to crime?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, there was a lot of crime in Kosovo, and the further west you went, the worse the crime got.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, isn't that your hesitancy to call the KLA terrorists and refer to their acts as terrorist acts? You now want to call them crimes?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, the criminality and the terrorism were very, very closely linked and intertwined. Many of the -- many of the resupply routes over the border from Albania were, to my knowledge, supply routes that had been used for smuggling for years and they were just being used to run guns at this stage. And when they no longer need guns, they would have gone back to running whatever else they were running.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness, it may be best that he not testify with his notes in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a particular document you have there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm writing myself notes as I go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In relation to the questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've written down ACTORD waging modern war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are notes that you've compiled as the evidence has been proceeding? Are they or are they notes that were prepared before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the note I've written today. Those are the notes I wrote yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's no reason why you shouldn't make notes as the evidence goes along.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 65 of your statement you -- you talked about -- and yesterday you talked about concern that VJ was conducting training exercises in the vicinity of KLA-held villages which you described as an intimidating thing. What I'm wondering is why -- why in the view of the OSCE was there something wrong with the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia conducting exercises on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia just because it might stir up a KLA person or two? What's wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Because there had been agreement that they were going to stay in barracks and there would only be outside barracks to the tune of three companies in locations that were defined in the agreement with General Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So then what you said yesterday is wrong, because your position yesterday was that they should have been conducting their training exercises somewhere else instead of near a KLA-held village where they would intimidate the KLA. What I'm wondering is why does that make any difference to you? What business does KLA have holding that village anyhow? That's the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. They're terrorists. They've taken over a village. Why are you supporting them and saying you shouldn't intimidate these poor terrorists taking over a village.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The reason we were there was because the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia appeared unable to keep its own house in order, and that was why we'd been asked to come in. And what we were trying to do was to make sure that things were not done that made the situation worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, from the evidence that you've given so far, I think it's fair to conclude that it was not VJ presence that made the situation worse. It was VJ absence, because when they were absent, the KLA would take over the territory. So as time went by, the territory kept being surrendered to the KLA and surrendered to the KLA, and, you know, pretty soon, if it kept going that way, they would have the whole province. And they had no business doing that. At best they were insurgents.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Agreed. Agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you'll also agree that when these exercises were going on, that if the KLA had not fired at them, there wouldn't have been any problem in the first place. It was the KLA firing at these exercises that caused the problem.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe we can talk a little bit about global stuff because you wanted to when you came in this morning. One of the problems that we see going on, if you just look at the newspapers, even today's International Herald Tribune is the asymmetrical nature of some of these modern conflicts where you've got a conventional army like the VJ was going up against a bunch of terrorists who tend to operate out of villages and from among civilians, and it makes for a very dicey situation to dry to deal with, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's a fairly common tactic for these terrorists or insurgent organisations to operate from within civilian enclaves, to carry out attacks from there and then when the army attacked exercises, its right of self-defence, and attacks that area, then you find no insurgents. You find no KLA. You find no people like that. And then there's a big claim that they're attacking civilians. That's a pretty common tactic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you're aware of the importance of that road that ran between Nis and Pristina?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. It was described as the lifeline.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel Ciaglinski called it the main resupply route and the main transit route or road route between Kosovo and the rest of the Serbia.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you called it the umbilical cord to Belgrade. Paragraph 76 of your statement. I take it, understanding how important that road was, that you certainly wouldn't take the position that the VJ should have just let the KLA take control of that road.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, General, I think I'm going to stop asking you questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Drewienkiewicz. I am Mr. Petrovic's [as interpreted] attorney. I shall ask you a few questions regarding your testimony given so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we should clarify that since your efforts to introduce yourself seem to have been undermined by the translation. This is Mr. Petrovic who is acting for Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is really not of the size of importance for the subject of our conversation, so I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I will continue in a bit of a different vein in respect of what you talked about with Mr. Ackerman a couple of minutes ago. You are certainly aware of document marked 5395 [as interpreted] here. This is a statement by the Yugoslav government, i.e., an agreement between the Yugoslav government and Wesley Clark at that moment. So could we have that document, please, on the screen in e-court, please. Please be so kind as to take a look at it and possibly agree with me, namely, that the essence of what was the request addressed to the Yugoslav side, which is contained in items 1, 2, 3 and so on of this document, which are pages 2, the bottom of the second page, and page 3.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't have it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: P395. P395, not 5395. So the document is P395. So document P395. Would you be so kind as to take a look at page 2 and page 3 in e-court. We shall disregard the first page for the time being. So we shall deal with pages 2 and 3. The gist of the request addressed to the Yugoslav side is that the police units, that's item 1, and the army units, that's item 3, should be withdrawn from Kosovo, those units of the police and the army which were deployed there after February, 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. I agree, it's 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Of course 1998. Please take a look at item 7 of this document. This item 7 describes -- or, actually, sets the deadlines for the withdrawals and deployments, namely, that it should be done by the 27th of October, 1998, by 1200 hours. Is that correct? Is this what item 7 contains of the document? And then it goes on to say that KDOM shall be informed about the new numbers. This is the gist of item 7, and this agreement was something on the basis of which you, inter alia, came to Kosovo. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, although we'd started to deploy after -- before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. So today, answering the questions of my colleague, Mr. Ackerman, you said that the essence of your duties in Kosovo -- one of your basic duties was, inter alia, to establish whether Serbian, i.e., Yugoslav forces, had been reduced to the required level from February, 1998. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we now please show the witness document marked 2D10. 2D10, which is -- this document is a statement by the Secretary-General of the NATO after a session of the northern alliance held on the 27th of October, 1998. I hope that we shall be able to see the document presently on the screen. This is a document under serial number 25. Can we see the bottom of the page, the last paragraph on the left side of the page. So this is a statement by the Secretary-General of NATO given on the 27th of October, which to say, after the expiry of this deadline that we saw here in this agreement that we saw a minute ago, and it says: [In English] "aerial surveillance assets and the Kosovo diplomatic observer mission have been very fined with Mr. Milosevic's actions matched the commitments he made to us. I'm pleased to report that over past 24 hours over 4.000 members of the special police have been withdrawn from Kosovo. Police and military units that are normally based in Kosovo are now moving back to their barracks together with their heavy weapons. Check-points can be dismantled. In addition, most police and military units that are normally based elsewhere in Yugoslavia have left Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, happy. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is: [In English] "The security forces are returning to the level ... [Interpretation] Let me just read once again the last sentence. [In English] ... they were at before the present crisis began." [Interpretation] My question, Mr. Drewienkiewicz, is this: First of all, do you know who verified the withdrawal of the forces and units of the police and the army to the level from February, 1998, and do you agree that that verification in this particular situation was carried out by KDOM?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, because we weren't on the ground in sufficient numbers, and I would observe that the NATO statement says most and are returning to the level. It doesn't say they have returned to the level. And it was our job when we got there to make sure that the process had continued, and to do that, I keep coming back to the baseline and to the reports and the paragraph 8 of the Wesley Clark agreement that we were just looking at mentioned all of these detailed weekly reports that we were going to get, none of which we ever got. So the statement that the Secretary-General of NATO made I'm sure was correct at the time. I completely believe it. And it says that most has happened, and they are returning to the level. It doesn't say they have, and we were never able to prove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it is your position that at that particular point in time, on the 27th of October, Serbian and Yugoslav forces had not fulfilled what was agreed under the agreement, what was requested of them under the agreement which we just saw, which is to return to the 1998 level, February, 1998 level. Is that what you claim?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming. I'm reading what the Secretary-General of NATO said, which is before me. It says at the bottom of the page: "The security forces are returning to the level they were at before the crisis -- present crisis began." I've been a scripter for senior people to know that if he'd meant the security forces have returned, they would have said they have returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it is your assertion that Yugoslavia, Serbia and Kosovo were not bombed in 1998 despite the fact that they had not met the requirements from the agreement that had been signed a couple of days before that.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It's my assertion that one of the things we were put in to do was to carry on that process. That's why we were called the Kosovo Verification Mission. And we really wanted to do that so that we could give you a clean bill of health.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, we are going to look at another document on the same page, and this is a statement of Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, also given on the same day, 27th of October, and the number of the document is 26. I have highlighted a few parts which I consider are of relevance.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, just slow down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And then I'm going to read the second part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I doubt if you need to read it. The witness is able to read both -- meets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to draw the witness's attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the second part where Madeleine Albright says and contends that the army units brought into Kosovo have been withdrawn. So there is no reference to any partial withdrawal, conditional withdrawal, such -- what see says is "Army units brought into Kosovo from outside have been withdrawn." That's what she says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Kofi Annan said that as well. There's no distinction. He said that most police and military units that are normally based elsewhere in Yugoslavia have left Kosovo. But it's the other point that the witness has just drawn your attention to, that progress is being made towards placing heavy weapons in storage. The units are -- the Kosovo-based units are moving back to their garrisons. So both say the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is exactly what this is about. There are statements by most authoritative persons who claim that Yugoslavia had met its obligation, its commitments from the agreement. However, as I can see that it is time for our break, I'm not going to belabour the point right now, but you will see as we proceed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If there is a point arising from this on which you wish to challenge the witness at the moment, do it now before we have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So first, was this verification done by KDOM on one part and on the other part by the NATO Verification Mission, the verification which is the subject of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: What happened in late October and was reported by KDOM and NATO was not my responsibility. My responsibility was to confirm the situation and to confirm that it was not changing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, why do you confirm a situation that has been confirmed, that is clarified? KDOM and the NATO Verification Mission confirmed the Yugoslav parties' actions in keeping with the agreement. Why a subsequent or additional verification of something that had already been done? That is the essence of my question?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, I think what you're saying is why put the Kosovo Verification Mission in if it was all a done deal, and the answer was that people senior to me and senior to you, sir, agreed it. So we got on with it. And our job was to verify against a baseline which we never got according to weekly detailed reports that we never received. So we were at something of a disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Drewienkiewicz, that the point's a rather narrow one that's being made, and that is that if this was happening, the baseline must have been established by the KDOMs before you got there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not receive that sort of information from any of the KDOMs, and we understood that, at the end of October, the units that lived outside -- that were based outside Kosovo had withdrawn, that the units had gone back to barracks, and the police had left Kosovo, the ones that had been brought in. So we understood that as at the end of October that was the case. Where we were at a loss was to know what that -- what was left, what -- what was left? What did it look like?
