How many police were there? Where were they? In what police stations? Where were the units? That was the information we needed, we asked for, that should have been in these detailed reports that we were supposed to get according to the Clark agreement, and we never got. And we kept asking for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we will break there. Could you, as has been the practice so far, leave with the usher, please, and we will resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, immediately before the break, answering a question by His Honour Judge Bonomy, you said that you had not received any information from KDOM regarding the baseline of the members of the army and police and the armaments. You are certainly acquainted with this agreement that we call the Jovanovic-Geremak agreement which is P658. And can we see the P658 agreement on the e-court, and would you please be so kind as to look at item 1.5 which says, "KDOM shall be acting on behalf of the Verification Mission until it is established." How is it possible, Mr. Drewienkiewicz, that you did not get information from KDOM when KDOM is an entity, which under the agreement between the OSCE and the Yugoslav party, acted on behalf of the mission pending its establishment?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, KDOM wasn't an entity in its own right. KDOM -- was it the UK KDOM, the American KDOM, the Russian KDOM, the French KDOM or the Canadian KDOM, I don't know. We certainly asked for this information from everybody we -- we saw. There had been a very big changeover of personnel within the KDOMs over this period. As we came in, they went out. And there were not very many people left in the KDOMs generally who had been there in the summer and until the end of October, so we were not able to get this information. We therefore went back to the originators of the information and said, we haven't been able to get this information. Please give it to us. It's in everybody's interest. And to this day, I do not understand why that was so difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, please be so kind as to give me specific replies to my questions. So KDOM then had not fulfilled the obligations it had undertaken under the contract, under the agreement, because it is -- it says here that the KDOM will act in place of the mission pending its establishment, until it is up and running. That is one thing. And secondly, did you have personal contact with the people who were in charge of the US KDOM, of the EU KDOM, the British KDOM? Did you know those people?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I think the people to whom the information must have been given was US KDOM, and they were the people who had the greatest degree of turbulence as they changed over people as we came in, but at no stage was I given or were anyone -- any people in the KVM given any reports by any of the KDOMs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you know a man by the name of Shaun Byrnes, and did you cooperate with that person? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: He was the head of the US KDOM, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have meetings with that man? Were you ever together during your mission in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: We met quite frequently, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And did you ask that person where the proof was, where the verification of the baseline checking which they had done was? It would be only normal that you should have asked him for that. You here have a trip to Belgrade, a trip to Pristina, or comments, objections, and you are not asking for information from the man who is supposed to have that information and was in fact under the obligation to refer such information to you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically going to Shaun Byrnes and specifically asking him. I do recall that at the time he was not actually in Kosovo very much, and I don't think I met him until mid-December.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the US KDOM acted in contravention of the agreement OSCE Yugoslav side. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that. I mean, that's argumentative, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now. Tell -- it might be more helpful if you have the information to tell the witness what the baseline was now so that we can see if in fact there was a significant piece of information being kept back or not rather than this argument over formality, which, you know, makes it very clear why the whole place appears to have blown up eventually.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The degree of detail that we got was much less than we felt we needed. We felt we needed to know what the weapons, what the units -- what the weapons were in each location, what the unit holding was. What we really wanted was the serial number of every tank, so that if a tank appeared, we could check that it genuinely was a Kosovo-based tank and so on. Now, that degree of detail was what we asked for in the meetings in -- in the meeting in Belgrade, and it was also referred to in the letter that Ambassador Walker wrote to -- to Milosevic at the time. That was not the degree of detail that we got. We eventually got, at our suggestion, not at the suggestion of the Yugoslav side, a copy of the arms control declaration under what's called Article 4 of, I think, the Vienna document, which was very much more brief. It just said the total number of heavy weapons with a calibre above 12.-something millimetres held in each location and what the type was. This was -- this was the information that was exchanged under the conventional forces in Europe agreement and was far less detail then we wanted and we only got that -- well, we had it, but we had access to it through Vienna. And therefore we went to the Yugoslav side and said, "We propose to use this if you're not prepared to give us anything else," and they said, "Okay." We never got any detail of where the police stations were, what their manning was, what their rotation was, because police units were being rotated in and out of Kosovo from the rest of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would really like to ask you to reply specifically to my questions, if possible. If not possible, then tell me so and I will rephrase the question in order to get short answers, because we won't get very far as we're proceeding now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Until that answer, your questions were longer than the answers the witness was giving, if you just have a look at the transcript. And that I found a very helpful answer, I may say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with the assumption that KDOM transform into the Verification Mission as had been envisaged under the agreement, or rather, had the KDOM transformed eventually into or been absorbed into the Verification Mission, then baseline would not have become an issue at all because it was the KDOM that raised the issue of baseline?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, because it was different people. I'm perfectly willing to accept that I should have pressed much harder with everybody I met from every KDOM to see who the mysterious person was who was given the baseline. I'll acknowledge that publicly. I should have done it. I didn't. And having not done it, I went to the people who presumably had given the baseline and said, "Could you give us a copy as well," thinking that that was a very quick way to overcome the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your reports, did you inform the Vienna centre of the fact that you did not have the information you requested from KDOM, that they refused to provide the information? Did you put that down in your report?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't say they refused. I said we specifically didn't go to them and say, "Please give us the reports," because there'd been so much changeover of personnel in the KDOMs that it was very difficult to find somebody who admitted to being there in late September. And as I say, which KDOM was it? I'm pretty sure you're talking about the US KDOM, but it was a confusing time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, who was the information given to and in what form?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is precisely the problem, that the information had not been given. KDOM had not been integrated into the Verification Mission, and the information that KDOM had concerning baseline that had been set down on the 27th of October --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's my question. It's relating to the information given to KDOM. Who was the information given to in KDOM, which KDOM, and in what form was it given?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, KDOM carried out verification through its -- well, I'm now supposed to testify on matters that I am not versed in. I will give you my understanding of view. After the signing of agreement, KDOM carried out verification and established that police and military units were withdrawing from Kosovo. He -- or, rather, they informed respective embassies accordingly and their governments, and it was as a result of that that the suspension had been done. So it was KDOM, with the help of the NATO Verification Mission from the area, that had carried out the verification and informed the governments, and as a result, the decision to go ahead with the bombing was suspended. It was on the basis of this that the governments of the Western countries made the decision to suspend bombing. This decision and the evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Try to do what you've invited the witness to do and stick to the question. You're saying, I assume from that, that it was not the obligation of the FRY to provide this detail, that it was up to KDOM to get it for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot go into the details or the specifics of your question. I can tell you this: KDOM had credible information as to the withdrawal having been done. I cannot tell you how KDOM arrived at the information. I can merely tell you that KDOM had information that was suitable to base the NATO decision upon not to go ahead with any bombing. And of course, if you'll allow me, the information -- or, rather, KDOM had to arrive at that information with full cooperation on the Serb or Yugoslav side. Otherwise, it would not have been possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a sort of meaningless statement that doesn't assist us. We are not prepared to sit here dancing round formality. We want to get on with establishing what the actual facts of the matter were. So in the circumstances where you really don't have a basis for this cross-examination, let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will move on. I must say that I do not share this position, but I do not want to belabour the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, tell me what it is that you're saying was the obligation of the FRY. You say you can't tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the obligation was to withdraw the forces of police and army that had arrived in the area of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. The obligation we're talking about is provision of information about the location of and sizes of the forces and their weaponry. Now, what obligation did the FRY have to give that to either KDOM or the KVM? Did they have no such obligation according to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the state had the obligation to meet the requirements or the undertakings it had taken upon itself. KDOM and Verification Mission were the other parties, and there's nothing more than that. The agreements that we speak of do not imply that verifications of weapons had to be carried out. This is not contained in the agreements. This is what the witness is saying here whilst interpreting the part of the agreement relating to the freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your position is, as I think suggested three times now without getting a clear answer, that the FRY had no obligation to give this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, now that we are discussing the matter, the state was a signatory to the subregional arms control agreement. According to this arms control agreement, which the FRY fully complied with, all the information that are subject of your interest were regularly reported to OSCE. This is the gist of what we're talking about. The KVM did not have the jurisdiction to verify weapons. It was through other organs and pursuant to another agreement that this should have been done, and the FRY fully cooperated with OSCE organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All I am asking you about is the baseline. I want to know whether your client accepts that the FRY had or did not have an obligation to inform either the KDOM or KVM of the baseline statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is our position that the Verification Mission was not entitled to verify armaments in the barracks or other installations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question. Just stop and move on with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look at document P440. I would kindly ask you to look at page 4 of the document and tell me, first of all, do you recognise the document? Are you familiar with the document?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Sorry, can we go back to the -- I am not aware of what this document is at the moment. It was eight years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You can take a look at page 2 of the document. This is the agreement between NATO and the Chief of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia at the time, Perisic, concerning the NATO Verification Mission. Please look at --

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Look at page 4, the last paragraph on that page, wherein the obligations of the Yugoslav side are defined concerning the removal of anti-aircraft weaponry from Kosovo and their storage in depots. It is also stated here, as one can well see, that the locations of the depots will be known and that they will be open for inspection. My question for you is as follows: When the sides are willing to arrange an inspection of a barracks, isn't this the precise way in which they do arrange the matter, directly and in a straightforward manner, and not through the agreements wherein the freedom of movement would allow for inspection? Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I agree that this is the agreement between FRY and NATO, and the fact that we were neither of those parties meant that when we declared or proposed how we were going to operate, we did so in a very specific way, in a very transparent way. We were very detailed about the way we were going to operate. Now, if something had given particular difficulty, then it could have been discussed. No discussion ever took place. Ambassador Walker's letter to the FRY was never replied to. So we went from a -- a very detailed letter to nothing, and that was where we had great difficulty, and that was why we wouldn't let it drop, because we didn't think that it was an appropriate response when we had put it -- been put into this -- into Kosovo at extremely great expense, at extremely great difficulty to the sending nations that we should just be cold shouldered like this. What was the point of putting in a Kosovo Verification Mission if it wasn't able to verify? We were not particularly ornamental.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, is: Sides -- two sides, when they're arranging for an inspection of a depot or a barracks, would they do it explicitly as had been done in this NATO agreement with the Yugoslav side or in some other way? Would you agree with me or not, or let's move on?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, it was two separate entities. The -- we were not working for NATO and NATO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, that's not the point that's being put to you. This is being put to you as an example of a far better way of arranging things. So could you address that issue. The counsel is saying to you that if arrangements are being made for an inspection, this is the way to do it rather than the vague terms of the agreement that your mission had. Now, do you want to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't agree with that. We were put in, as I say, to verify. We wanted to verify that things that we were aware of were as they should be. Presumably for that reason, there had been the various agreements like the agreement between Clark on returning to barracks, on regular reporting. The agreement with Byrnes on the number of check-points that were going to be occupied by the MUP. These are all things we will needed to follow up on to confirm that the situation was whatever it was. So we cannot rely on air verification. If you're going to do air verification, then the NATO-FRY air verification agreement is, I'm sure, a very good one. We weren't an air verification mission. We were a ground verification mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If there existed this sort of dispute with the Yugoslav side already, if there existed a dispute concerning the true contents of the document, is it true that some of the mission, the OSCE mission officials proposed that a conference be organised where the disagreements would be resolved? Is it true also that at a certain point in time you also thought this to be an expedient way of solving matters?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I certainly hoped that that was -- sorry. Got it. I certainly hoped that in the wake of the -- after the meeting in Belgrade with General Ojdanic that the next step was going to be the meeting in Pristina with the commander of the Pristina Corps to work out the modalities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand my question? I apologise for interrupting you. My question was: Did any of the members of the OSCE mission propose that a conference be held where the disagreements or misunderstandings would be resolved, and did you support this idea? That's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: A simple answer. Of course everybody wanted everybody to sit down and have meetings and discussions and resolve the difficulties, yes. That is why I wanted to meet the commander of the Pristina Corps. And I didn't get to meet him because it was forbidden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Petrovic, the document you've placed on the screen, does that amount to saying that NATO could enter the sites where weapons had been stored and do the job that the KVM were apparently having difficulty doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand that that is so. Indeed, that this agreement, indeed authorises NATO to do so. And as far as I know, it was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was the problem about allowing KVM to do it, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just don't know the answer that to question. I've tried to, but I haven't been successful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I attempt to help, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you think you can, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think what NATO had the -- the authority in this document to do was to inspect weapon and cantonment sites outside Kosovo, that weapons had been withdrawn from Kosovo into cantonment sites, i.e., in the remainder of FRY, and that they could then be inspected by NATO away from Kosovo. There were certainly no NATO teams inside Kosovo on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's, I don't think, what it says. It says that the conditions apply within Kosovo. And if you read the main part, it said all SAMs and air defence weapons will either be removed from Kosovo or placed in cantonment sites and not operated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were never any NATO individuals on the ground inside Kosovo, and it was not my understanding in the meetings I had with the people on the air verification mission that they intended or thought they could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I am awaiting for the translation, Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to my question whether anybody from the OSCE launched an initiative for a similar conference, you cannot give me an answer, so I will move on.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you not understand the answer given to be that it was a matter to be discussed with the Pristina Corps command and that was prohibited? Is that a separate thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, it is a separate issue, and we shall be leading evidence to that effect in due time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Leading evidence to what effect? At the moment, I don't understand what you're getting at, and it's important we understand what you're doing. You're putting questions about a proposal for a conference. Have you got some specific information that there was such a proposal that you want to challenge the witness with, and if so, if you don't ask him specific questions, we won't understand what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Bo Pellnas launch an initiative for a conference to be held where the situation would be clarified? Did you support such an initiative, and did that initiative fall through because of Walker's interference?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Bo Pellnas was our man in Belgrade, and he came -- he set up the meeting with the -- with the FRY General Staff. So he came with me, as I remember it, to the FRY General Staff. And so he and I probably spoke every day or every other day, and certainly if -- if in the wake -- in -- after the meeting with the General Staff, he would have been part of the discussions that were going on about how we could sit down with -- with whoever was prepared to sit down with us to get this information. So I'm sure he was going around proposing a conference. I'm not aware that the initiative fell through because of Walker's interference, because Walker was fully informed at every stage what was going on and was fully supportive. He had signed the letter that we sent to FRY saying this is how we want to carry out inspections. And so I reported back to him at least once a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, when the KLA is in question, did you at any stage attempt to verify their armaments, to verify their units, to verify the areas in which they were carrying out training, in which they were based? Did you ever attempt to do that during any stage of your stay in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. If I can take those in -- in order. We wanted, and we said we were going to check up on their armaments because we were very keen, for instance, to know if they had surface-to-air missiles, because it was of a prime concern to us if we were going to get a medevac helicopter in. So we did feel we wanted to know how well they were armed. So we were going to go up to all of the hilltops where they were and make the best assessment we could, remembering that this was -- these were not fully formed units under command with a -- with a table of equipment and a manpower strength in the same way that a regular unit would be. So to verify what armaments they had, yes. To verify their units, yes. To get an idea of what their capability was, where they were, to verify the areas in which they were based, yes, we did. I can remember schematic maps of Kosovo in which we -- we put on what we call duck eggs, circles to show the areas where the KLA were definitely, the areas where they operated occasionally, and the areas where they did not operate. I can remember doing that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you do that in the way that was to be done vis-a-vis the Yugoslav forces? Did you write down the numbers of -- the serial numbers of the heavy weaponry of the rifles, the sights, where the training was being conducted, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They didn't have any heavy weaponry at this stage. The heavy weaponry I wanted the serial numbers of were things like tanks. They didn't have any. The locations where they were, yes. We did note all that down. And we took GPS with us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your answer was that you were going to check up on their armaments. Did you never get that job done for one reason or another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it took us a long time, sir, to get -- to get into their locations. But when we did, what we did was put people into their locations that lived with them, and they reported back to me on the general level of training, of where they were, of what their sort of numbers and what their capability was. It wasn't an arms-control inspection because they weren't a force that was amenable to that, so we weren't able to say, "Please give us how strong your unit is and what its equipment is," because they weren't -- they weren't that sort of unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we mustn't, I think, lose sight of two things. One, the nature of the KLA for a start; and secondly, that they weren't party to the agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. We got reminded of that several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you compile any reports on where they were based, how many of them there were, where they were doing exercises? Is this part of your report?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: We did produce some documents on that. They were not -- they were not particularly widely circulated because they had grid references in that might have been of use to -- to -- to ill-disposed people. But, yes, we did produce documents. They weren't doing exercises. I mean, guerrilla units don't do exercises. They -- they sit on the top of the hill until they decide they're going to come down in order to do something. That's not an exercise. That's -- that's a guerrilla operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And where were these reports distributed? Are there any such reports among this batch of documents that we saw during these last two days?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can certain -- I -- in digging through the stuff in my garage, I've certainly come across documents on KLA attitudes and some of the maps with where the KLA were and where they weren't. So they existed. They were not made widely available. They were made available on a need-to-know basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were they submitted to the OSCE headquarters in Vienna? Were they part of the reports which were prepared for the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Some of the maps with the KLA locations on it were part of a PowerPoint briefing that was given to the chairman in office when he came down. We did not regularly submit full reports on the KLA to the permanent council because we operated with the KLA on the basis of acceptance, and in order to be accepted, one of the things that we were quite keen we were not to do was to give away their positions to people who might take advantage of it. We were trying to be neutral in this, and in order to get that access, certain restrictions were placed on us and we had to restrain ourselves in some areas. So, no, we didn't pass all this information up to the OSCE permanent council, and no, it wasn't distributed everywhere within the mission. And because we respected those confidences, we were able to stay inside the KLA camps and have access to them and be able to attempt to influence them to be -- to be more restrained, which we couldn't have done if we had posted up their locations in a public place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if you did not send it to Vienna and to New York, to whom did you send that information? Where did that information go to?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It stayed inside the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: With what purpose, with what objective, to be used for what? Was that your mandate, to collect information and retain it for your own use? Was this envisaged by your mandate? So information about one of the sites would remain behind closed doors?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. My mandate was, above everything, to keep the mission together and to keep the members of the mission safe, and I was not going to recklessly do things that were going to endanger the members of the mission, and nor did the permanent council want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So your mandate was to inform on one side, and what you collected about the other side and related to the same subject matter would remain for your internal use, if I understand your position correctly.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The mandate was the mandate of the OSCE-FRY. There was no agreement with the Albanians. And that mandate was what we were sent down to do. We were expecting that there was going to be an agreement with the Albanian side, and that was why Chris Hill, the American ambassador, was down there. And I can assure you that when I was assigned to this job and I was shown the agreement and I saw that it was only with one party, I said, "What the heck's the deal with the -- with the KLA, with the Albanian side?" And they said, "Don't worry. It's being fixed by -- by Ambassador Chris Hill." And that remained the case until mid-December when he admitted he wasn't going to get an agreement, and by that stage, we were down there and we were starting to operate. At that stage, possibly the OSCE should have reconsidered what it had let itself in for, but that was a matter for the OSCE. By that stage, I was doing my best to get this mission up and running as quickly as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a couple questions more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I only have several questions regarding a helicopter which -- to which reference was made several times. I hope that I will not ask too much, just five or six questions with your permission. But believe me, in view of the importance attached to the helicopter by the KVM, that importance is also reflected on us, so that I hope that I will not overdo it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So yesterday you said that the litmus test of the Serbian will to cooperate with the KVM was the question of helicopters. You also said that it was so important that it was a symbolic question, that it was the first area where we got a direct reply -- rather, a direct refusal from the Serbian side. I'm asking you this: Is it true that when you raised the question of -- that at the time when you raised the question of helicopters, was it true that throughout Kosovo there were at different levels tens, scores of meetings, and I repeat, at different levels where information was exchanged which were actually the very substance and reason for your sojourn in Kosovo? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: There were -- there were plenty of meetings going on. This was -- this was early December, so there were only about -- I would say there were less than 150 people in the KVM on the ground at this stage, and so there weren't scores of meetings. Everyone was trying to set themselves up, and we were not getting information. We were seeking information, and we were generally not getting very helpful information. We were detecting an atmosphere of lack of cooperation which was why these things were being elevated to the level of the head of mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. My second question is, the aircraft that had been announced by the KVM, were they allowed to land at the Pristina airport and elsewhere in the territory of FRY without any limitations but those that are normally imposed by air control? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. There were flights into Pristina airport by a civilian aircraft that had been chartered by the OSCE to -- to move heavy equipment up and down, and these movements into Pristina airport were fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you offer a modification of the agreement pursuant to which you were present in the FRY in order to include the use of helicopters for evacuation purposes? Was there such a proposal advanced on your part?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't needed because aircraft -- the word "aircraft" includes helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who would be responsible for the safety and security of the helicopter concerned in the event of an incident in the Yugoslav airspace in terms of regulations governing air navigation? Who would have been responsible in that event?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It would have had to have followed the normal air traffic control rules that presumably would have come out of Pristina airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the Yugoslav side would have been responsible for each and every such incident; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, which incident? If a helicopter had come in, then it would have obeyed -- for flight safety reasons, it would have obeyed the instructions given to it by ground control in wherever the controlling ground control was. That's what helicopters do. That way they didn't bump into each other or bump into mountains. If you're saying were we --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I'll answer the questions. I won't try to suggest your questions to you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: One more question. You stated yesterday that you were never offered a white helicopter bearing the insignia of the Red Cross. And had you been offered something along the lines, you would most likely have accepted the offer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. We would -- let me take that one piece at a time. We were offered the -- the ability to contract a Yugoslav casivac helicopter, casual evacuation helicopter. I was not told it was either white or bore the insignia of the Red Cross, but my understanding of those casualty evacuation helicopters was that they were normal service helicopters in effect with a stretcher strapped into them. That was not what we were seeking. We were seeking a fully-equipped medical evacuation helicopter that you didn't have, or we weren't aware that you had, and you certainly never made it clear -- the Yugoslav side never made it clear that you had. And the reason we were so insistent on this was because the permanent council in Vienna were extremely concerned at the safety of their verifiers, to the extent that we were not getting the verifiers turning up, and this was really very serious. People were frightened to come because of the TV coverage. Every time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you covered most of that yesterday. Let's move on, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your microphone, please, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Ackerman asked you [In English] Big Red Cross on it, would you still reject it?" Your answer was: "It was never offered like that."

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But the answer would probably be [Interpretation] we would have looked at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you said you would have probably rejected it. And I think that that's the end of that matter for the moment. What else do you want to ask, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness stated something else yesterday, but this will be quite clear from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My note is he was never offered a white helicopter with a big Red Cross. If he had been, he would probably have rejected it, and he did not ask if he could paint it orange. Now, are you saying that's an inaccurate note?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 7833, I might have been mistaken, but it says: "[In English] But the answer would probably have been yes, because one of the reasons," [Interpretation] and so on and so forth. I may have been mistaken, but this is on page 7833.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You would still reject it but the answer would -- sorry, let me get it. Yeah. "It was never offered like that, but the answer probably would have been yes." Which I understood was it would probably have been rejected. Now, you better clarify this since we seem to have a different understanding of this, Mr. Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, if -- if we had been offered a helicopter with the same capability as the one that we had hired, then we would certainly have considered it. I did have a -- a medical expert who knew about these things, and I would have got him to crawl over it and say is this up to specification. We would still have been concerned if it was carrying -- if it was bearing Yugoslav army markings because nobody would know who was in it, and that would have been a prime concern of mine because the safety of the verifiers was very important to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, let's try and clarify this question that was put to you yesterday as well. Were you offered, for the purposes of medical evaluation, a white painted helicopter bearing the symbol of the Red Cross? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, not put like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm merely trying to put to you a part of the testimony by Colonel Ciaglinski, whom I believe you are acquainted with, who stated quite the opposite. This is page 6880, where you were asked -- he was asked, "Were you offered such a helicopter?" And his answer was, "Yes. We did not take the offer for other reasons, but it was offered to us." And that was Mr. -- or, rather, Colonel Ciaglinski's testimony before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, let me be clear. First of all, I was in charge of this matter; he wasn't. He was an observer. We were offered verbally quote, I think, "one of our army medevac helicopters." To the best of my knowledge, they were operating without the red cross, not white, and were just a normal military helicopter with a stretcher strapped into them, and I wasn't prepared to consider that low-level of medical assistance, particularly when we'd already got one that was much better, that was sitting in Macedonia, simply waiting to be called forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: General, I'm Norman Sepenuk. I'm attorney for General Ojdanic. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I'm going to start with the first meeting that you had with your staff on November 23, 1998. It was your opening meeting that you had with them. And in a moment, I'm going to put the record of that meeting up on the screen, but take my word for it if you would just for a moment that one of the questions that was raised at that meeting, and I take it -- and this is in your handwriting, I believe, and we confirm this -- can confirm this in a moment, is what do we call the KLA. Do you remember that, sir? Do you remember that from your notebook?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I'm sure that that was a question that we asked many times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And you testified in the Milosevic trial that your own practice was to refer to the KLA as "the insurgents," and then, "which I felt described them in a way that was accurate but not emotional." Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And Mr. Milosevic, on cross-examination, asked you, "Did you know at the time the kind of people you were communicating with and cooperating with? Were you aware of that?" And he was referring to the KLA. And you said, "We were well aware that they were an insurgent organisation, and we were well aware that they were killing policemen, and at no stage during our time in Kosovo did we ever condone the killing of policemen." And then Mr. Milosevic asked you another question, "Do you consider them to be a terrorist organisation or an insurgent organisation?" And your answer was, "I think insurgent is a better word because it is less emotive." Emotive. And Mr. Milosevic said, "And you consider that 'terrorist' is an emotional and emotive word, do you?" And you were answer was, "Yes, I do." Now, the other day, I forget whether it was yesterday, but the other day, Judge Bonomy threw out, at least for discussion, the notion that perhaps you didn't want it -- when I say "you," OSCE didn't want to refer to KLA as terrorists because somehow that would set up a barrier to effective communication, that if you call somebody a terrorist, they're not exactly likely to take to you. Now, that was Judge Bonomy's notion that he threw out, and of course you've already rated Judge Bonomy and the trial panel a 1 when it comes to reliability, and all the Defence teams join that -- tell the panel. And I'd like to know your opinion now on that, on Judge Bonomy's notion. Again, he just threw it out for discussion.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I think I stand by what I said in 2002. We were having to make contact with the KLA. We had a lot of Kosovar Albanians working for us, and indeed we had Kosovar Serbs working for us inside our headquarters. And so the way we discussed things among ourselves was bound to be reported back along the Serb channels and along Albanian channels. So unless we specifically went for a walk in the park, we assumed that people were listening to us all the time. And so we tried not to -- we may not always have succeeded, but we tried not to describe the parties to this disagreement that was going on in Kosovo in ways that were going to make our life more difficult. Now, we were having to put people up into the KLA positions to earn their trust and confidence, so that they would talk to us, so that we could attempt to influence them without any formal agreement, but on the basis of a degree of trust that had been built up. To do this, I had to have two separate sets of liaison people, those that dealt with the Serbs and those that dealt with the KLA. But the last thing I wanted was for someone to turn up at a KLA location and to have -- and it be confronted by the fact that we're constantly referring to them as terrorists and in derogatory terms back down inside our offices. So we were cautious, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation, General. And in any event, while you were trying -- you personally were trying to diffuse the emotionality of the word "terrorist" by using the term "insurgent," the fact is that this was indeed an emotional and emotive issue for the Serbs, including the VJ, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I had this conversation several times with General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And -- and I think, General, that you appropriately recognise the importance of the -- of Kosovo in Serbian history and any impact the KLA would have on that by a note you made in your notebook. And I would ask the usher to put up 3D412, page 300. Thank you, that's fine. General, you recognise that as a page out of your notebook, and is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And there are -- there are four numbers appearing on the upper left-hand corner of that document, and it says "FRY," and underneath the four numbers, underneath is the numbers 1389. Now, I'm allowed to ask leading questions on cross-examination, but I'm not going to. I'm going to ask you as if I was questioning you on direct examination. Tell us what 1389 means, please, and tell us what, if anything, you said about 1389 to your assembled staff.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: 1389 is the date of the battle on the field of the blackbirds, which is an extremely significant anniversary for the Serb people. I think I -- I think this particular page is my notes to myself for standing at Brezovica talking to a new consignment of verifiers arriving. And so these would -- we've already found that I -- I write myself little notes so that I don't get completely confused. And this would have been -- this would have been those. So this was lesson one to people arriving off the plane in Skopje, some of whom who had never been in the Balkans before, who had not necessarily done any pre-deployment training, and they were about to go into an extremely delicate situation. So I needed to give them, in about half an hour, what their country should have given them in about six weeks before they deployed, and this was my attempt to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And essentially the message I take it you were trying to convey was that Kosovo has a very important, really, a special role in Serbian history, a role of almost mythical proportions, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd go along with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And given the threat of the KLA, whether you call them terrorists or insurgents, it doesn't matter, given the threat of the KLA, you very appropriately at that meeting -- and if the usher would scroll up a bit on the page. Keep scrolling up a bit, please. That's it. You can stop. You very appropriately posed the fundamental question which in a sense is what this trial is all about, General, and that is what can the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia do as a sovereign state to defend itself? An important question indeed; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And that was a particularly crucial question at the time since the KLA, as we all know, was not a party to any of the three basic agreements, the one of October, 1998, the so-called Clark-Naumann Agreement signed by Mr. Milosevic; the MUP agreement, signed by Mr. Byrnes; and finally, the agreement setting up the OSCE operation, the KLA not part of any of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And at this time, November 23rd, 1998, you're already aware that the Serbian side had honoured that part of the Clark-Naumann Agreement which required the VJ and the MUP to withdraw forces from Kosovo to reach the levels existing in February, 1998. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They had only until the end of October. What we had been seeking to find out was what had been going on since then, if anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. But they initially --

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that they initially did comply; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm certainly happy with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you also learn, at least by this time, November 23, 1998, that all these positions that had been abandoned by MUP and by the VJ were then reoccupied by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Not at this stage, no. That -- it wasn't as quick as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It was gradual, then, and it took place over a period of time, but it did take place, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You've so testified?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: But I would add that on November the 23rd, I think I'd -- I'd actually been back in Kosovo maybe four days. I'd come down in October. I'd then gone back to -- to Vienna, and we had -- we'd been setting up the KVM. We'd been starting to procure the vehicles, the radios, to call for the people to be brought forward, and I'd been on that until I was asked to go -- come down to Kosovo and to implement the plan that I'd just been writing. And I think I came down on the 20th of November. So how much of all that did I know on the 23rd? Not as much as I know now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But I take it that there was at least some and rather substantial reoccupation of positions. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say substantial. I would say that the reoccupation of the positions was starting to be observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And it became substantial and as a matter of fact, you protested that to the KLA and they chose to ignore you. Is that a fair statement? That's what you testified to.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean I personally went into their lines and above Podujevo, into that position, and talked to the local men on the ground and said, You're crazy. If you're going to do this, then you're giving the other side an excuse to come and -- to come after you. You need to get out of here because otherwise you -- you will be in danger. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So by the time you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly make pauses between questions and answers for the interpreters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You got that message, did you, Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're going to break a bit earlier. So just finish when it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'll break whenever the Court wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just finish the question you were about to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: By the time you met with General Ojdanic on November 27, 1998, you already knew that it was -- there was at least some evidence, if not overwhelming, at least some evidence that the central premise, a central premise of the 25 October, 1998 agreement was just wrong, and that is the initial sentence of the undertaking by the Yugoslavian government saying -- recognising United States [sic] Security Council Resolution 1199 and proceeding from the fact that organised terrorism has been defeated in Kosmet and that all actions against terrorists have ceased as of September 29, 1998, the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- and then there's a series of undertakings, withdrawal by the MUP, withdrawal by the VJ -- and you knew, did you not, sir, that the -- this notion of organised terrorism being defeated in Kosmet just wasn't so. That was wishful thinking and turned out not to be true. Isn't that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I would say that at the time we were very skeptical that the KLA were going to be as restrained as you describe, and at this time, of course, we were still waiting on the -- the Chris Hill agreement that we were all hoping was going to be something that would -- would bind the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, my last question then is and very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you learned, though, very shortly at that time, sometime in early December, that there was not going to be an agreement because the KLA had threatened to kill any Albanian who signed an agreement with Mr. Hill that would somehow limit the activities of the KLA. Isn't that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how I heard it, how we heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: This is an appropriate time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Drewienkiewicz, would you go, please, with the usher. And we will resume at 5 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: General, my questions before the break were at least in part designed to place in some context the meeting you had with General Ojdanic and his staff on November 27, 1998, and we've already established that there was at least some reoccupations of positions abandoned by the MUP and by the VJ, and at the very least, the KLA wasn't showing any particular inclination to enter into my kind of political agreement. I think that's where we are. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd go along with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And so what I'd like to do is direct your attention to the meeting itself. Now, the meeting did take place on November 27, 1998, in Belgrade, and you'll recall that General Ojdanic had only be appointed a few days before; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: As Chief of the General Staff. So he was new in the job.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. And I think you described the tone and mood of the meeting as fairly neutral; right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you said in your testimony yesterday, since General Ojdanic had only very recently taken up his position just a few days before, "We knew that meant we were going to get less out of the meeting because we knew that he would have had less time to be briefed and that he would be less inclined to make decisions at the meeting, so we went into this meeting with lowered expectations, I would say." Correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But as a matter of fact, would you agree that there were a number of positive developments that took place at that meeting? And I'll get to them now.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And if you take a look at OTP Exhibit 2535, which has already been shown to you but was discussed only generally and I'd like to go into a bit more detail. If the usher would put that on the screen, 2535. Can you read that -- yeah, there we go. Okay. And at the top there, in the first paragraph, General Ojdanic stated that "The Yugoslav army would fulfil all of their obligations and tasks under the FRY-OSCE agreement;" correct? That's your notes.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what he stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And General Ojdanic identified a desire to be transparent about troop rotations for Kosovo. "They are a normal part of Yugoslav army operations and should not be misunderstand by international community." That's also what he said; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And further, going down just a bit. Yes, just move -- just move up. Thank you. As is outlined in the letter from Ambassador Walker, "We need information on all security forces in Kosovo. General Ojdanic ensured that the first piece of information about Yugoslav army forces was provided before 1 December, the same information about Yugoslav army forces providing under the terms of the agreement on subregional arms control." That was said also; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And then a little bit down. Go down a little bit further. No, go actually up a bit. Go back the other way, please. Yes. Right there. It says, "We are now waiting --" no. Go up just a bit more. I'm sorry. Keep going. Keep going. Okay, stop there please. "We are now waiting for an indication from General Ojdanic as to when the rest of the required information about army elements will be provided. Alternatively, and if this meets with the approval of General Ojdanic, it may be easier for the corps commander to provide it directly to me." Correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That was what I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, please, 3D412, page 318. And could you go up a bit, please. That's fine. Thank you. And you say toward the middle of the page, "You may note," I guess this is General Ojdanic speaking. No, I believe it's you, General. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: This is my note for the next meeting, the one that didn't take place. So this is my -- my no-brain note for myself. It's my speaking note.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In other words, you wanted to use -- but the short of it was, you wanted to use the Pristina Corps unit as the testing ground for the KVM inspection procedures; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And then on the subject of troop rotation, going down just a little bit -- scroll up just a bit, please. Okay. That's fine. On the subject of troop rotation, General Ojdanic mentioned the scheduled early December rotation of Yugoslavia army forces for Kosovo. He said, "We understand that this is normal part of Yugoslav army operations and usually takes place every three months." And he went on to say, "It is the FRY's interest to ensure sufficient transparency about the process so that local residents and the international community can be assured of the normality of the rotation." And let me make one amendment here, General. I think that was you making those comments.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, those three bullets points were my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: So the preamble -- this was this was to help me in a meeting that didn't take place, but my preamble would have been to mention that General Ojdanic mentioned this rotation and we, the KVM, understand that this is a normal part of Yugoslav army operations. It is all -- and those three bullets would have been the words that I put into my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And the short of it is that General Ojdanic agreed completely on this point. That's what you have in your notes; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I was attempting to talk this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: And this meeting didn't take please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, CNN, what is that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: This was the discussion that we had where the gist of the discussion was the last thing that anybody of us wants is for there to be busloads of soldiers being seen coming into Kosovo as part of the rotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you, General. Excuse me for that.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All I want to know -- you have CNN, I think, in other places.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What is CNN? What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: We didn't want a CNN cameraman standing by the side of the road photographing a bus full of Yugoslav soldiers and quickly getting onto the 6.00 news that the -- the Yugoslavs are breaking the terms of their agreement by reinforcing with new units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You know, General, I caught 1389, but I didn't catch CNN. Sorry. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It's an American disease.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Now -- so you left the meeting with General Ojdanic, as you testified yesterday, thinking that things had gone sufficiently well to be able to follow up on this; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You'd say -- you testified, "I would say that I left the meeting with General Ojdanic feeling that there was a basis for future cooperation. I didn't expect to be dealing with him on a day-to-day basis because he was sitting in Belgrade with other responsibilities than just Kosovo obviously. And so what I wanted was to go to him and to get him to issue an instruction to the Pristina Corps commander to deal directly with me and then only to raise things to the level of the Belgrade Ministry of Defence if events proved impossible or too difficult down on the ground." Correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then just a few days later, on December 2, 1998, you wrote a letter to General Ojdanic, and that is 2543. If that could be put on the screen, please. Prosecution Exhibit 2543. And you -- you said, "I would like to -- to General Ojdanic, "I would like to let you know how much I appreciated the fact that you took time to meet with me." You went on to say that you welcomed the information provided on Yugoslav army forces on 29 November. "I take note of the fact that you have provided the information as we agreed, and I will inform the head of mission of this positive development." Correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you further went on to say, "I will also consult with the Pristina Corps commander regarding the rotation of Yugoslav army personnel that you mentioned when we met, so that we'll be able to verify the nature of this activity as well. Then, finally thank you once again for demonstrating your correct attitude with regard to KVM and I look forward to other productive meetings in the future." Correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- during the briefing that you had or the proofing that you had with Mr. Marcussen and others, in that supplemental statement, little paragraph (e), you said, "During the meeting on 25 November," it's actually, I think, a mistake. I think it should mean -- it means 27 November. Let's just assume that. During the meeting on 27 November 1998, General Ojdanic did not say no KVM inspections and you left the meeting with him thinking that the next meeting would be with the Pristina Corps to implement further details regarding inspections to establish a baseline. But you didn't receive the information you wanted because it turned out there was a difference of interpretation between the OSCE and the Serbian political leadership as to what was required under the agreement. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, my last two matters, General, are -- I'm told to slow down, so I'll do that. The last two --

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I'll try to say, yes, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, I was told to slow down, General, not you. The last two matters that I have are contained in your statement. Now, you didn't testify about this, but I'm -- I have to ask you about it, because under the Rules of the Tribunal, your statement is also admitted into evidence, so we have to deal with it. And I'm looking at paragraph 65 and 66 and, General, I note an inconsistency between -- have you had time to locate them? Let me wait until you locate them.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I note, at least what appears to me, to be an inconsistency between those two paragraphs, perhaps indicating, at least I hope indicating, frankly, a misunderstanding or a failure of communication between you and the Prosecutor's office, and let me be specific. In paragraph 65, you expressed the need to know the training area boundaries and Ojdanic stated that my request was noted, which was something of a standard reply for him. My first question -- I may have missed it. There are hundreds of pages in your notebooks. But my first question is, where does that appear in your notes, the fact that General Ojdanic noted your request? It may be in your notebook, but I have not been able to find it.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I -- I cannot put my finger on it. I mean, this is a statement I wrote in -- in June 2000 and went through in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Can you conceive that maybe you just might have gotten that one wrong?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I -- that -- I would need to crawl over it, and I'm prepared to say I might have got that wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And then if we'll go on to page -- to paragraph --

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. That was part of that conversation with Ojdanic. I would need to check my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. But absent that or absent quite frankly anything coming from Mr. Marcussen, if you're at least prepared at this point, General, to say maybe you got it wrong. I won't belabour the point and I'll go on to the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Okay. I'm -- yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And on page -- paragraph 66, you're talking about rotation of conscripts in and out of Kosovo, and General Ojdanic had previously said at the meeting that he was willing to give you information about that, put aside for a moment that you never received it to your satisfaction because of the falling through of the inter-meeting with corps commander, but General Ojdanic said he was willing to at least initially to give you that information, but you said this was not noted but flatly refused by Ojdanic and refused with considerable authority. And again, General, I have combed over your notes, and -- I may have missed it, but I don't see anything in your notes that is even close to that statement that you're making, and I'm guessing, General, that that's another one that somehow showed up in your statement but really wasn't said by you.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I think it was said by me. The question is was it part of that meeting or was it part of another meeting. Both the -- the content of 65 happened and the content of 66 happened. Was it in that meeting or was it in a subsequent meeting with General Loncar quoting General Ojdanic? That's what there's doubt in my mind, and I think it may be that at a subsequent meeting with General Loncar, he said that this was not to be allowed, and he took General Ojdanic's name as the issuer of the order. Now, that's the best I can do without going through my notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. So at least -- at least at this point you're willing to amend your statement that it wasn't General Ojdanic who said this to you, but it may have been General Loncar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure it was General Loncar quoting General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So that's an amendment to your statement. And that, of course, is not what happened at your meeting. At your meeting, General Ojdanic -- it was a very open meeting and he indicated that he would be willing to provide that information; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think that's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If you allow me just to wait for translation on B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Drewienkiewicz. My name is Djuro Cepic. I am Defence counsel here, and I will be putting questions to you. In your statement in paragraph 186, you say -- or, rather, in 176, you said that in late February, 1999, you toured the border area, and yesterday, during the examination-in-chief by my learned friend Marcussen, you gave your positions that are in annex 7, which is Exhibit P640. In this document you gave the following assessment: In order to secure the border, 6.600 men would be required, which tallied with the assessments held by the VJ at the time. This is my question: Do you know how many VJ soldiers secured the state borders at the time?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I wish I had. That brings me back to my question of the baseline.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What would you tell me if I were to tell you that at that point in time only 3.282 soldiers were engaged in securing the border, which is a number that is far lower than the number actually required for the job?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be surprised, because the Yugoslav army were not managing to -- to stop people coming over the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Drewienkiewicz. Now that we are dealing with the border area, in your statement and in the course of your yesterday's evidence, you mentioned the indents which took place on the 14th of December, 1998, when several members of the KLA were killed and several were captured. In paragraph 86 of your statement, you say that the patrols of the Kosovo Verification Mission photographed bodies but never saw any prisoners. This statement of yours where they never saw any prisoners, was this the reason why on the meeting on the 16th of December, 1998, you refused to contact Verification into this incident or concerning this incident?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Sorry, give me that again. I thought we worked rather hard on this incident. What didn't I do?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] It is a bad translation, actually. [Interpretation] I will try to rephrase my question. After the incident, did you at the meeting on the 16th of December, where Mr. Walker was present as well, refuse to verify the incident because none of your verifiers had ever seen prisoners anywhere on any occasion?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. We did verify the incident, and we said that we thought that this was a legitimate action by the VJ in response to a clear breach of the cease-fire by the KLA, and I think we said that publicly to both Walker and Holbrooke who was there at the time. We did quite a long report on it, and -- because it involved having to walk about four miles in through the snow, we thought we'd done rather well to do this. I think there was one prisoner photographed in retrospect, but we didn't get access to the prisoners that we were told had been taken. And we asked for access, but we didn't get it until much later in January. I think that was the main point of contention at the time. Other than that, it was seen as a fair cop by the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Drewienkiewicz. Before I put my question to you, could I ask Mr. Registrar to show the Defence Exhibit 39470. Sir, are you familiar with the member of the Kosovo Verification Mission, a member of the British metropolitan police sergeant Henri Young?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Young, I think. I remember the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's get the exhibit. Is it one of your own exhibits Mr. Cepic? It's been brought up as a number that doesn't exist. Is it a 5D or a 3D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And I kindly ask you paragraph 38, please. Actually, that is a page number 6, and would I like to mark on paragraph 35, and then later on 38, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
